claim: Defective 3β-hydroxysterol-Δ7-reductase (DHCR7) in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS) results in a deficiency in cholesterol and accumulation of 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC).
source: Defective 3β-hydroxysterol-Δ7 -reductase (DHCR7) in the developmental disorder, Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS), results in a deficiency in cholesterol and accumulation of its precursor, 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known consequence of DHCR7 deficiency in SLOS, supported by established scientific knowledge about the disease.

claim: Loss of DHCR7 causes accumulation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterol metabolites in murine or human cortical neural precursors.
source: Here, we show that loss of DHCR7 causes accumulation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterol metabolites, premature neurogenesis from murine or human cortical neural precursors, and depletion of the cortical precursor pool, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in Figure 2 showing accumulation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterols in Dhcr7-/- cortices and SLOS patient-derived cells.

claim: Loss of DHCR7 causes premature neurogenesis from murine or human cortical neural precursors.
source: Here, we show that loss of DHCR7 causes accumulation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterol metabolites, premature neurogenesis from murine or human cortical neural precursors, and depletion of the cortical precursor pool, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 3 showing increased βIII-tubulin+ neurons in Dhcr7-/- and SLOS NPCs.

claim: Loss of DHCR7 causes depletion of the cortical precursor pool both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Here, we show that loss of DHCR7 causes accumulation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterol metabolites, premature neurogenesis from murine or human cortical neural precursors, and depletion of the cortical precursor pool, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1, 5, and 6 showing decreased Ki67+ and Pax6+ precursors in Dhcr7-/- cortices.

claim: 3β,5α-dihydroxycholest-7-en-6-one (DHCEO) is a major oxysterol that mediates the neurogenic effects of DHCR7 loss.
source: We found that a major oxysterol, 3β,5α-dihydroxycholest-7-en-6-one (DHCEO), mediates these effects by initiating crosstalk between glucocorticoid receptor (GR) and neurotrophin receptor kinase TrkB.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing DHCEO treatment replicates the premature neurogenesis phenotype.

claim: DHCEO initiates crosstalk between glucocorticoid receptor (GR) and neurotrophin receptor kinase TrkB.
source: We found that a major oxysterol, 3β,5α-dihydroxycholest-7-en-6-one (DHCEO), mediates these effects by initiating crosstalk between glucocorticoid receptor (GR) and neurotrophin receptor kinase TrkB.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figure 8C showing DHCEO treatment increases phosphorylation of both GR and TrkB.

claim: Loss of DHCR7 or direct exposure to DHCEO causes hyperactivation of GR and TrkB and their downstream MEK-ERK-C/EBP signaling pathway in cortical neural precursors.
source: Either loss of DHCR7 or direct exposure to DHCEO causes hyperactivation of GR and TrkB and their downstream MEK-ERK-C/EBP signaling pathway in cortical neural precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figures 5J-K and 8A showing increased phosphorylation of GR, TrkB, MEK, and C/EBPβ.

claim: Direct inhibition of GR activation with an antagonist rescues the premature neurogenesis phenotype caused by loss of DHCR7.
source: Moreover, direct inhibition of GR activation with an antagonist or inhibition of DHCEO accumulation with antioxidants rescues the premature neurogenesis phenotype caused by the loss of DHCR7.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 8D showing RU38486 (GR antagonist) rescues the neurogenesis phenotype in DHCR7-KD cells.

claim: Inhibition of DHCEO accumulation with antioxidants rescues the premature neurogenesis phenotype caused by loss of DHCR7.
source: Moreover, direct inhibition of GR activation with an antagonist or inhibition of DHCEO accumulation with antioxidants rescues the premature neurogenesis phenotype caused by the loss of DHCR7.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 8E-J showing vitamin E, vitamin E/C, and GSH rescue the neurogenesis phenotype and reduce DHCEO levels.

claim: Brain cholesterol contributes to 25% of total cholesterol in the human body.
source: Brain is rich in cholesterol, contributing to 25% of total cholesterol in the human body, and nearly all cholesterol in the brain is synthesized locally (Dietschy and Turley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dietschy and Turley, 2004.

claim: Nearly all cholesterol in the brain is synthesized locally.
source: Brain is rich in cholesterol, contributing to 25% of total cholesterol in the human body, and nearly all cholesterol in the brain is synthesized locally (Dietschy and Turley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dietschy and Turley, 2004.

claim: Dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism in CNS can potentially cause significant defects in CNS development and functions.
source: Therefore, dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism in CNS can potentially cause significant defects in CNS development and functions.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference from the importance of cholesterol in the brain and is supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Enzymatic deficiencies in cholesterol biosynthesis cause a number of inherited diseases with severe neurodevelopmental phenotypes.
source: Indeed, enzymatic deficiencies in cholesterol biosynthesis cause a number of inherited diseases with severe neurodevelopmental phenotypes (Porter and Herman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Porter and Herman, 2011.

claim: SLOS is an autosomal recessive, neurological and developmental disorder characterized by multiple developmental defects.
source: Smith-Lemli Opitz syndrome (SLOS) is an autosomal recessive, neurological and developmental disorder characterized by multiple developmental defects, such as distinctive facial features, cleft palate, microcephaly and holoprosencephaly, as well as severe intellectual impairment and behavioral problems (Porter and Herman, 2011; Thurm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Porter and Herman, 2011 and Thurm et al., 2016.

claim: SLOS patients display a high incidence (>50%) of autism spectrum disorders.
source: Notably, SLOS patients display a high incidence (>50%) of autism spectrum disorders (Bukelis et al., 2007; Sikora et al., 2006; Tierney et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bukelis et al., 2007; Sikora et al., 2006; and Tierney et al., 2006.

claim: SLOS is caused by mutations in the DHCR7 gene.
source: SLOS is caused by mutations in the 3β-hydroxysterol-Δ7 -reductase gene (DHCR7), which encodes the enzyme that converts 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) to cholesterol in the final step of the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway (Fitzky et al., 1998; Tint et al., 1994; Wassif et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fitzky et al., 1998; Tint et al., 1994; and Wassif et al., 1998.

claim: DHCR7 encodes the enzyme that converts 7-DHC to cholesterol in the final step of the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway.
source: SLOS is caused by mutations in the 3β-hydroxysterol-Δ7 -reductase gene (DHCR7), which encodes the enzyme that converts 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) to cholesterol in the final step of the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway (Fitzky et al., 1998; Tint et al., 1994; Wassif et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fitzky et al., 1998; Tint et al., 1994; and Wassif et al., 1998.

claim: Defective DHCR7 leads to deficiency in cholesterol and accumulation of 7-DHC in tissues and fluids of affected individuals.
source: Defective DHCR7 resulting from the mutations leads to deficiency in cholesterol and accumulation of 7-DHC in tissues and fluids of affected individuals (Tint et al., 1994; Tint et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tint et al., 1994 and Tint et al., 1995.

claim: 7-DHC is highly reactive toward free radical oxidation, leading to the formation of oxysterols.
source: 7-DHC was found to be highly reactive toward free radical oxidation, leading to the formation of its oxidative metabolites, that is oxysterols (Xu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2013; and Xu et al., 2011.

claim: 7-DHC-derived oxysterols can exert cytotoxicity in neuronal cells.
source: 7-DHC-derived oxysterols can exert cytotoxicity in neuronal cells, induce gene expression changes, and increase formation of dendritic arborization from cortical neurons (Korade et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Korade et al., 2010 and Xu et al., 2012.

claim: 7-DHC-derived oxysterols can induce gene expression changes in neuronal cells.
source: 7-DHC-derived oxysterols can exert cytotoxicity in neuronal cells, induce gene expression changes, and increase formation of dendritic arborization from cortical neurons (Korade et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Korade et al., 2010 and Xu et al., 2012.

claim: 7-DHC-derived oxysterols increase formation of dendritic arborization from cortical neurons.
source: 7-DHC-derived oxysterols can exert cytotoxicity in neuronal cells, induce gene expression changes, and increase formation of dendritic arborization from cortical neurons (Korade et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Korade et al., 2010 and Xu et al., 2012.

claim: Increased dendrite and axon formation has been observed in neurons isolated from Dhcr7-KO mouse brain.
source: Interestingly, increased dendrite and axon formation has also been observed in neurons isolated from Dhcr7-KO (Dhcr7-/-) mouse brain (Jiang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2010.

claim: Cholesterol, 7-DHC, and oxysterols derived from both have been found to play important roles in modulating signaling pathways in developing tissues and organs.
source: Cholesterol, 7-DHC, and oxysterols derived from both have been found to play important roles in modulating signaling pathways in developing tissues and organs, such as Hedgehog (Hh) and Wnt signaling pathways (Byrne et al., 2016; Corcoran and Scott, 2006; Huang et al., 2018; Myers et al., 2017; Porter et al., 1996; Raleigh et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Byrne et al., 2016; Corcoran and Scott, 2006; Huang et al., 2018; Myers et al., 2017; Porter et al., 1996; and Raleigh et al., 2018.

claim: Ring-B oxysterols derived from 7-DHC oxidation inhibit Smo in the Hh pathway.
source: Related to SLOS, ring-B oxysterols derived from 7-DHC oxidation inhibit Smo in the Hh pathway (Sever et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sever et al., 2016.

claim: Cholesterol was recently found to selectively activate canonical Wnt signaling over non-canonical Wnt signaling.
source: On the other hand, cholesterol was recently found to selectively activate canonical Wnt signaling over non-canonical Wnt signaling (Sheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sheng et al., 2014.

claim: In human induced pluripotent stem cells derived from SLOS patient fibroblasts, accumulation of 7-DHC was found to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin pathway.
source: However, in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from SLOS patient fibroblasts, accumulation of 7-DHC was found to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin pathway, which contributes to the precocious neuronal specification in SLOS neural progenitors (Francis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Francis et al., 2016.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt/β-catenin pathway contributes to precocious neuronal specification in SLOS neural progenitors.
source: However, in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from SLOS patient fibroblasts, accumulation of 7-DHC was found to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin pathway, which contributes to the precocious neuronal specification in SLOS neural progenitors (Francis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Francis et al., 2016.

claim: Oxysterols have been shown to bind and activate signaling molecules and nuclear receptors, including estrogen receptors, liver X receptors, and glucocorticoid receptor.
source: Depending on the position of the oxidation, oxysterols have also been shown to bind and activate other signaling molecules and nuclear receptors, including estrogen receptors, liver X receptors, and glucocorticoid receptor (GR), and thus, play important roles in neurodevelopment and diseases (DuSell et al., 2008; Theofilopoulos et al., 2013; Voisin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DuSell et al., 2008; Theofilopoulos et al., 2013; and Voisin et al., 2017.

claim: Dhcr7 mRNA is expressed in embryonic day 11 (E11) through postnatal day 0 (P0) cortex.
source: RT-PCR analysis showed expression of Dhcr7 in embryonic day 11 (E11) through postnatal day 0 (P0) cortex (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dhcr7 mRNA expression is stable from E11 to E18.
source: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) also suggested the stable expression of Dhcr7 from E11 to E18 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dhcr7 protein is present in the developing cortex.
source: Western blot analysis further confirmed the presence of Dhcr7 protein in the developing cortex (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dhcr7 is broadly expressed in the developing cortex and is detectable in precursors in the E12 ventricular and subventricular zones (VZ/SVZ).
source: Immunostaining showed that Dhcr7 was broadly expressed in the developing cortex and was detectable in precursors in the E12 ventricular and subventricular zones (VZ/SVZ) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Dhcr7+ cells in E12.5 cortical precursor cultures are co-labeled with the precursor markers Sox2 and Pax6.
source: In the E12.5 cortical precursor cultures, Dhcr7 + cells were co-labeled with the precursor markers, Sox2 and Pax6.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data described in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Dhcr7 is co-labeled with the neuronal marker βIII-tubulin and the neural lineage marker Nestin.
source: Dhcr7 was also co-labeled with the neuronal marker, βIII-tubulin, and the neural lineage marker, Nestin.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data described in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Dhcr7 is consistently expressed in neural lineage cells.
source: The results suggested that Dhcr7 was consistently expressed in neural lineage cells, which is consistent with our in vivo analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-labeling data showing Dhcr7 expression with various neural markers.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 alleles causes a significant decrease in the proportion of Ki67+ precursors in E12.5 cortical precursor cultures.
source: Cultures were immunostained for Ki67 and βIII-tubulin 3 days after plating, which revealed that loss of Dhcr7 caused a significant decrease in the proportion of Ki67 + and Pax6+precursors whereas increased the proportion of βIII-tubulin+neurons (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 alleles causes a significant decrease in the proportion of Pax6+ precursors in E12.5 cortical precursor cultures.
source: Cultures were immunostained for Ki67 and βIII-tubulin 3 days after plating, which revealed that loss of Dhcr7 caused a significant decrease in the proportion of Ki67 + and Pax6+precursors whereas increased the proportion of βIII-tubulin+neurons (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 alleles causes a significant increase in the proportion of βIII-tubulin+ neurons in E12.5 cortical precursor cultures.
source: Cultures were immunostained for Ki67 and βIII-tubulin 3 days after plating, which revealed that loss of Dhcr7 caused a significant decrease in the proportion of Ki67 + and Pax6+precursors whereas increased the proportion of βIII-tubulin+neurons (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 alleles does not affect the survival of cortical precursor cells in culture.
source: Immunostaining for cleaved caspase 3 (CC3) showed that the loss of Dhcr7 alleles did not affect the survival of cortical precursor cells in culture (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by CC3 immunostaining data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 leads to premature neurogenesis and decreased proliferation of cortical precursors.
source: These results suggested that loss of Dhcr7 leads to premature neurogenesis and decreased proliferation of cortical precursors.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data showing decreased Ki67+ cells and increased βIII-tubulin+ cells.

claim: Significantly fewer number of neurospheres are generated from Dhcr7-/- embryonic cortices compared to Dhcr7+/+ littermates.
source: Significantly fewer number of and smaller neurospheres were generated from Dhcr7-/- embryonic cortices compared to its Dhcr7+/+ littermates (Figure 1L–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurosphere assay data shown in Figure 1L-M.

claim: Smaller neurospheres are generated from Dhcr7-/- embryonic cortices compared to Dhcr7+/+ littermates.
source: Significantly fewer number of and smaller neurospheres were generated from Dhcr7-/- embryonic cortices compared to its Dhcr7+/+ littermates (Figure 1L–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by neurosphere assay data shown in Figure 1L-M.

claim: There is an approximately twofold decrease in the number of secondary spheres from Dhcr7-/- cortical precursors relative to Dhcr7+/+.
source: The results showed that there was an approximately twofold decrease in the number and diameter of secondary spheres from Dhcr7-/- cortical precursors relative to Dhcr7+/+ (Figure 1N–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by secondary neurosphere assay data shown in Figure 1N-O.

claim: There is an approximately twofold decrease in the diameter of secondary spheres from Dhcr7-/- cortical precursors relative to Dhcr7+/+.
source: The results showed that there was an approximately twofold decrease in the number and diameter of secondary spheres from Dhcr7-/- cortical precursors relative to Dhcr7+/+ (Figure 1N–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by secondary neurosphere assay data shown in Figure 1N-O.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 alleles disrupts the proliferation and self-renewal of cortical precursors.
source: Thus, the loss of Dhcr7 alleles disrupts the proliferation and self-renewal of cortical precursors.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the neurosphere assay data.

claim: DHCR7 immunoreactivity is detected in almost all Control hNPCs with Sox2+ and Nestin+ cells.
source: Immunoreactivity of DHCR7 was detected in almost all Control hNPCs in these cultures with Sox2 + and Nestin + cells (Figure 1P).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: The proportion of Ki67+ precursors is significantly decreased in SLOS NPC cultures compared to Control.
source: Notably, the proportion of Ki67 + precursors was significantly decreased whereas the proportion of βIII-tubulin+neurons were increased in SLOS NPC cultures, similar to the phenotype seen in murine cortical precursors from Dhcr7-/- embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data described in the text and shown in Figure 1Q-S.

claim: The proportion of βIII-tubulin+ neurons is significantly increased in SLOS NPC cultures compared to Control.
source: Notably, the proportion of Ki67 + precursors was significantly decreased whereas the proportion of βIII-tubulin+neurons were increased in SLOS NPC cultures, similar to the phenotype seen in murine cortical precursors from Dhcr7-/- embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data described in the text and shown in Figure 1Q-S.

claim: DHCR7 is involved in the proliferation and differentiation of human NPCs.
source: Taken together, DHCR7 is involved in the proliferation and differentiation of human NPCs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data from SLOS patient-derived NPCs.

claim: 7-DHC is highly susceptible to free radical oxidation.
source: 7-DHC is highly susceptible to free radical oxidation (Xu et al., 2009), which leads to the formation of numerous oxysterols in cells and tissues (Xu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2011; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2009.

claim: Free radical oxidation of 7-DHC leads to the formation of numerous oxysterols in cells and tissues.
source: 7-DHC is highly susceptible to free radical oxidation (Xu et al., 2009), which leads to the formation of numerous oxysterols in cells and tissues (Xu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2011; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2013 and Xu et al., 2011, and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: There is significant accumulation of 7-DHC in embryonic cortices from Dhcr7-/- embryos throughout cortical development from E12.5 to E16.5.
source: These analyses revealed significant accumulation of 7-DHC and reduction of cholesterol in the embryonic cortices from Dhcr7-/- embryos throughout cortical development from E12.5 to E16.5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is reduction of cholesterol in embryonic cortices from Dhcr7-/- embryos throughout cortical development from E12.5 to E16.5.
source: These analyses revealed significant accumulation of 7-DHC and reduction of cholesterol in the embryonic cortices from Dhcr7-/- embryos throughout cortical development from E12.5 to E16.5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 7-DHC oxysterols, such as DHCEO, 4α-OH-7DHC, and 4β-OH-7DHC, show substantial accumulation in Dhcr7-/- cortices, reaching up to 4-8 ng/mg of tissue.
source: Furthermore, 7-DHC oxysterols, such as DHCEO, 4α-hydroxy-7-DHC (4α-OH-7DHC), and 4β-hydroxy-7-DHC (4β-OH-7DHC) (Xu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2011) showed substantial accumulation in the Dhcr7-/- cortices, reaching up to 4–8 ng/mg of tissue, throughout the development (Figure 2A and C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4 ng/mg of tissue would translate into approximately 10 μM assuming the density of the brain is 1 g/mL.
source: Note that 4 ng/mg of tissue would translate into approximately 10 μM assuming the density of the brain is 1 g/mL.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the assumption of brain density.

claim: Cholesterol-derived oxysterols, such as 24-keto-Chol, 24,25-epoxy-Chol, 24- or 25-OH-Chol, 7-OH-Chol, and 7-keto-Chol decreased or did not change significantly in Dhcr7-/- cortices relative to Dhcr7+/+ cortices.
source: On the other hand, cholesterol-derived oxysterols, such as 24-keto-Chol, 24,25-epoxy-Chol, 24- or 25-OH-Chol, 7-OH-Chol, and 7-keto-Chol decreased or did not change significantly in Dhcr7-/- cortices relative to Dhcr7+/+ cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data described in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Significant accumulation of 7-DHC and 7-DHC-derived oxysterols and reduction of cholesterol were found in both SLOS patient-derived hiPSCs and NPCs relative to Controls.
source: Furthermore, significant accumulation of 7-DHC and 7-DHC-derived oxysterols and reduction of cholesterol were also found in both SLOS patient-derived hiPSCs and NPCs relative to Controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: DHCR7 mutations led to the accumulation of 7-DHC and 7-DHC-derived oxysterols in murine and human NPCs.
source: Taken together, DHCR7 mutations led to the accumulation of 7-DHC and 7-DHC-derived oxysterols in murine and human NPCs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the LC-MS/MS data from both murine and human cells.

claim: Dhcr7 shRNA2 significantly decreased the percentage of transfected cells expressing Dhcr7.
source: When cortical precursors were transfected with Dhcr7 shRNA2-EGFP, the shRNA significantly decreased the percentage of transfected cells expressing Dhcr7 (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Dhcr7 KD led to a significant decrease in the proliferation of cortical precursors as measured by Ki67 immunoreactivity 3 days post-transfection.
source: Dhcr7 KD led to a significant decrease in the proliferation of cortical precursors as measured by Ki67 immunoreactivity 3 days post-transfection or by adding 5-ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU) to culture 1 day post-transfection and immunostaining for EdU 2 days later (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Dhcr7 KD led to a significant decrease in the proliferation of cortical precursors as measured by EdU incorporation.
source: Dhcr7 KD led to a significant decrease in the proliferation of cortical precursors as measured by Ki67 immunoreactivity 3 days post-transfection or by adding 5-ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU) to culture 1 day post-transfection and immunostaining for EdU 2 days later (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: The significant decrease in precursor proliferation caused by Dhcr7 KD was caused by a decrease in Pax6+ radial precursors.
source: The significant decrease in precursor proliferation was caused by a decrease in Pax6 +radial precursors (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Dhcr7 KD led to a significant increase of βIII-tubulin+ neurons 3 days post-transfection.
source: Furthermore, Dhcr7 KD led to a significant increase of βIII-tubulin+neurons 3 days post-transfection, but it did not affect cell survival as examined by immunostaining for CC3 (Figure 3D, H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D and H.

claim: Dhcr7 KD did not affect cell survival as examined by immunostaining for CC3.
source: Furthermore, Dhcr7 KD led to a significant increase of βIII-tubulin+neurons 3 days post-transfection, but it did not affect cell survival as examined by immunostaining for CC3 (Figure 3D, H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by CC3 immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D and I.

claim: KD of Dhcr7 reduced EGFP+ multicellular clones.
source: KD of Dhcr7 reduced EGFP + multicellular clones (Figure 3K) whereas neuron-only (βIII-tubulin+) clones were increased (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: KD of Dhcr7 increased neuron-only (βIII-tubulin+) clones.
source: KD of Dhcr7 reduced EGFP + multicellular clones (Figure 3K) whereas neuron-only (βIII-tubulin+) clones were increased (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: KD of Dhcr7 decreased the number of precursors in clones containing at least one Sox2+ cell.
source: Furthermore, the number of precursors in clones containing at least one Sox2 + cell is decreased (Figure 3M).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Human DHCR7 cDNA showed significant rescue of the murine Dhcr7 shRNA KD phenotypes.
source: The human DHCR7 cDNA showed significant rescue of the murine Dhcr7 shRNA KD phenotypes, confirming that the neurogenesis and proliferation phenotype is Dhcr7 shRNA-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The neurogenesis and proliferation phenotype is Dhcr7 shRNA-dependent.
source: The human DHCR7 cDNA showed significant rescue of the murine Dhcr7 shRNA KD phenotypes, confirming that the neurogenesis and proliferation phenotype is Dhcr7 shRNA-dependent.
evidence: This is confirmed by the rescue experiments showing that human DHCR7 cDNA rescues the phenotype caused by murine Dhcr7 shRNA.

claim: KD of human DHCR7 reduced EGFP+ and Ki67+ proliferating precursors in human NPCs.
source: Human NPCs were transfected with this shRNA-EGFP and analyzed by immunostaining 4 days later (Figure 3O), which showed that the KD of human DHCR7 reduced EGFP + and Ki67 + proliferating precursors whereas increased EGFP + and βIII-tubulin+newborn neurons (Figure 3P–R), similar to those observed in murine cortical precursors and SLOS hNPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3O-P.

claim: KD of human DHCR7 increased EGFP+ and βIII-tubulin+ newborn neurons in human NPCs.
source: Human NPCs were transfected with this shRNA-EGFP and analyzed by immunostaining 4 days later (Figure 3O), which showed that the KD of human DHCR7 reduced EGFP + and Ki67 + proliferating precursors whereas increased EGFP + and βIII-tubulin+newborn neurons (Figure 3P–R), similar to those observed in murine cortical precursors and SLOS hNPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3O and Q.

claim: DHCEO-treated cortical precursors showed a significant increase in the proportion of βIII-tubulin+ newborn neurons.
source: Notably, DHCEO-treated cortical precursors showed a significant increase in the proportion of βIII-tubulin+newborn neurons and a significant decrease in the proportion of Ki67 + precursors (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: DHCEO-treated cortical precursors showed a significant decrease in the proportion of Ki67+ precursors.
source: Notably, DHCEO-treated cortical precursors showed a significant increase in the proportion of βIII-tubulin+newborn neurons and a significant decrease in the proportion of Ki67 + precursors (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The effect of DHCEO on cortical precursors was observed in a dose-dependent manner up to 3.5 µM.
source: This effect of DHCEO was observed in a dose-dependent manner up to 3.5 µM, which is roughly the concentration of DHCEO in the brains of P0 Dhcr7-/- mice (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4B-C and a citation to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: 3.5 µM is roughly the concentration of DHCEO in the brains of P0 Dhcr7-/- mice.
source: This effect of DHCEO was observed in a dose-dependent manner up to 3.5 µM, which is roughly the concentration of DHCEO in the brains of P0 Dhcr7-/- mice (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: There was no significant change in cell death/survival with DHCEO treatment.
source: There was no significant change in cell death/survival with DHCEO treatment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CC3 immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 4α-OH-7DHC treatment at a concentration of 2 µM displayed significant increases in βIII-tubulin+ neurons and decreases in Ki67+ precursors without significant changes in cell death/survival.
source: Interestingly, 4α-OH-7DHC treatment at a concentration of 2 µM also displayed significant increases in βIII-tubulin+neurons and decreases in Ki67 + precursors without significant changes in cell death/survival (Figure 4H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4H-J.

claim: Treatment with DHCEO at physiologically relevant concentrations completely replicated the premature neurogenic phenotype observed in murine and human SLOS NPCs.
source: To summarize, treatment with DHCEO at physiologically relevant concentrations completely replicated the premature neurogenic phenotype observed in murine and human SLOS NPCs while 4α-OH-7DHC may also contribute to the phenotype despite its toxicity at high concentrations.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data showing DHCEO treatment replicates the SLOS phenotype.

claim: 4α-OH-7DHC may contribute to the premature neurogenic phenotype despite its toxicity at high concentrations.
source: To summarize, treatment with DHCEO at physiologically relevant concentrations completely replicated the premature neurogenic phenotype observed in murine and human SLOS NPCs while 4α-OH-7DHC may also contribute to the phenotype despite its toxicity at high concentrations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the data showing 4α-OH-7DHC has some neurogenic effects at lower concentrations but is toxic at higher concentrations.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 led to a reduction of all cortical layers at E18.5.
source: The analyses showed loss of Dhcr7 led to a reduction of all cortical layers, resulting in the reduction of the overall size of the neocortex (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 resulted in the reduction of the overall size of the neocortex at E18.5.
source: The analyses showed loss of Dhcr7 led to a reduction of all cortical layers, resulting in the reduction of the overall size of the neocortex (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: There is a significant increase of Tbr1+ neurons in cortical sections from Dhcr7-/- mice at E14.5.
source: The analyses showed a significant increase of Tbr1 + neurons and Satb2 + neurons in the cortical section from Dhcr7-/- mice at E14.5 and E15.5, respectively (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: There is a significant increase of Satb2+ neurons in cortical sections from Dhcr7-/- mice at E15.5.
source: The analyses showed a significant increase of Tbr1 + neurons and Satb2 + neurons in the cortical section from Dhcr7-/- mice at E14.5 and E15.5, respectively (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5D and F-G.

claim: The majority of EdU-labeled cells migrated into the cortical plate in Dhcr7-/- mice at E15.5 after EdU injection at E12.5.
source: The majority of EdU-labeled cells migrated into the cortical plate in the KO mice, whereas EdU-labeled cells were scattered throughout the intermediate zone (IZ) and the cortical plates in the Dhcr7+/+ littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU labeling data described in the text and shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: EdU-labeled cells were scattered throughout the intermediate zone (IZ) and the cortical plates in Dhcr7+/+ littermates at E15.5 after EdU injection at E12.5.
source: The majority of EdU-labeled cells migrated into the cortical plate in the KO mice, whereas EdU-labeled cells were scattered throughout the intermediate zone (IZ) and the cortical plates in the Dhcr7+/+ littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by EdU labeling data described in the text and shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Relative to total TrkB, MEK1, and C/EBPβ levels, their phosphorylated forms increased in Dhcr7-/- cortices at E15.5.
source: This analysis showed that relative to total TrkB, MEK1, and C/EBPβ levels, their phosphorylated forms increased in Dhcr7-/- cortices (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 can dysregulate an RTK-dependent signaling pathway that is critical for neural precursor proliferation and differentiation.
source: This observation suggests that loss of Dhcr7 can dysregulate an RTK-dependent signaling pathway that is critical for neural precursor proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased phosphorylation of TrkB, MEK, and C/EBPβ in Dhcr7-/- cortices.

claim: The number of cells exiting the cell cycle in Dhcr7-/- cortices was significantly increased at E13.5 and E14.5 compared with Dhcr7+/+ cortices.
source: The index showed that the number of cells exiting the cell cycle in Dhcr7-/- cortices was significantly increased at E13.5 and E14.5 compared with Dhcr7+/+ cortices, indicating that loss of Dhcr7 increased cell cycle exit.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle exit index data described in the text and shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 increased cell cycle exit.
source: The index showed that the number of cells exiting the cell cycle in Dhcr7-/- cortices was significantly increased at E13.5 and E14.5 compared with Dhcr7+/+ cortices, indicating that loss of Dhcr7 increased cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell cycle exit index data.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the proliferating index in Dhcr7-/- cortices compared to Dhcr7+/+ cortices from E13.5 to E15.5.
source: The analyses showed a significant decrease in the proliferating index in Dhcr7-/- cortices compared to Dhcr7+/+ cortices from E13.5 to E15.5 (Figure 6C–D), indicating slower cycle progression and longer cycle length in Dhcr7-/- cortices (Chenn and Walsh, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation index data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: The decreased proliferating index indicates slower cycle progression and longer cycle length in Dhcr7-/- cortices.
source: The analyses showed a significant decrease in the proliferating index in Dhcr7-/- cortices compared to Dhcr7+/+ cortices from E13.5 to E15.5 (Figure 6C–D), indicating slower cycle progression and longer cycle length in Dhcr7-/- cortices (Chenn and Walsh, 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proliferation index data and supported by a citation to Chenn and Walsh, 2002.

claim: Accelerated depletion of the progenitor pool in Dhcr7-/- cortices results in decreases in the size of VZ/SVZ compared to Dhcr7+/+ cortices from E13.5 to E15.5.
source: Indeed, this accelerated depletion of the progenitor pool in Dhcr7-/- cortices results in decreases in the size of VZ/SVZ compared to Dhcr7+/+ cortices from E13.5 to E15.5 (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Pax6 immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Loss of Dhcr7 leads to a decrease in the overall number of cortical precursors with increased cell cycle exit and decreased proliferation index via activation of the RTK-mediated MEK-ERK-C/EBP pathway.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that loss of Dhcr7 leads to a decrease in the overall number of cortical precursors with increased cell cycle exit and decreased proliferation index via activation of the RTK-mediated MEK-ERK-C/EBP pathway.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data showing increased cell cycle exit, decreased proliferation index, and activation of the MEK-ERK-C/EBP pathway.

claim: 2357 genes were significantly differentially expressed in SLOS hNPCs relative to Control hNPCs (1072 upregulated and 1285 downregulated genes with adjusted p-value < 0.05).
source: Relative to Control hNPCs, 2357 genes were significantly differentially expressed in SLOS hNPCs (1072 upregulated and 1285 downregulated genes with adjusted p-value < 0.05), distinguishing the SLOS and Control precursors (Figure 7A; Supplementary file 6 for RNAseq data).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 6.

claim: The PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, MAPK signaling, and Ras signaling pathways are among those with the highest p-values in gene ontology and pathway analysis of SLOS hNPCs.
source: Gene ontology and pathway analysis found that the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, MAPK signaling, and Ras signaling pathways are among those with the highest p-values (Figure 7B–C; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 7B-C and Supplementary file 5.

claim: MAP2K1 (also known as MEK1) was found to be upregulated in SLOS patient-derived hNPCs.
source: Notably, MAP2K1(also known as MEK1) was found to be upregulated in SLOS patient-derived hNPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data described in the text.

claim: MAP2K1 is a key signaling molecule in MAPK and Ras signaling pathways, which are known to play important roles in precursor proliferation and differentiation.
source: MAP2K1 is a key signaling molecule in MAPK and Ras signaling pathways, which are known to play important roles in precursor proliferation and differentiation (Bonni et al., 1999; Ménard et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2013), consistent with the phenotypes that were observed in Dhcr7-/- mice and SLOS patient-derived hNPCs in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bonni et al., 1999; Ménard et al., 2002; and Yang et al., 2013.

claim: OCDO is a cholesterol-derived oxysterol that is structurally similar to DHCEO and is shown to bind and activate glucocorticoid receptor (GR).
source: Interestingly, 6-oxo-cholestan-3β,5α-diol (OCDO), a cholesterol-derived oxysterol that is structurally similar to DHCEO, is shown to bind and activate glucocorticoid receptor (GR) (Voisin et al., 2017; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voisin et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GR activation has been shown to activate TrkB.
source: Additionally, GR activation has been shown to activate TrkB (Jeanneteau et al., 2008), which leads to further activation of the RTK-mediated MEK-ERK pathway (Barnabé-Heider and Miller, 2003; Bartkowska et al., 2007; Ménard et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeanneteau et al., 2008.

claim: TrkB activation leads to further activation of the RTK-mediated MEK-ERK pathway.
source: Additionally, GR activation has been shown to activate TrkB (Jeanneteau et al., 2008), which leads to further activation of the RTK-mediated MEK-ERK pathway (Barnabé-Heider and Miller, 2003; Bartkowska et al., 2007; Ménard et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barnabé-Heider and Miller, 2003; Bartkowska et al., 2007; and Ménard et al., 2002.

claim: TrkB and RTK-mediated MEK-ERK pathway are necessary for neurogenesis during embryonic cortical development.
source: TrkB and RTK-mediated MEK-ERK pathway are necessary for neurogenesis during embryonic cortical development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Phosphorylation of GR was increased in Dhcr7-/- cortices compared to Dhcr7+/+ cortices at E15.5.
source: Western blots demonstrated that phosphorylation of GR was indeed increased in Dhcr7-/- cortices compared to Dhcr7+/+ cortices (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: DHCEO docks in the binding pocket of human GR favorably with a docking score of –9.
source: As seen in Figure 8B, DHCEO docks in the binding pocket of human GR favorably with a docking score of –9 (a negative value suggests favorable interactions), comparable to the docking score of OCDO at –9.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular docking simulation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The docking score of DHCEO is comparable to the docking score of OCDO at –9.5.
source: As seen in Figure 8B, DHCEO docks in the binding pocket of human GR favorably with a docking score of –9 (a negative value suggests favorable interactions), comparable to the docking score of OCDO at –9.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular docking simulation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: As GR phosphorylation increased, DHCEO-treated hNPCs also showed the phosphorylation of TrkB from 6 hrs to 10 hr exposure, which dissipated at 24 hr exposure.
source: As GR phosphorylation increased, DHCEO-treated hNPCs also showed the phosphorylation of TrkB from 6 hrs to 10 hr exposure, which dissipated at 24 hr exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data described in the text and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: DHCEO caused the increased phosphorylation of GR, which led to the activation of TrkB phosphorylation in human NPCs in vitro.
source: As no exogenous GR ligands and neurotrophins were added in these experiments, these results indicated that DHCEO caused the increased phosphorylation of GR, which led to the activation of TrkB phosphorylation in human NPCs in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course western blot data showing sequential activation of GR and TrkB after DHCEO treatment.

claim: Inhibition of GR by RU38486 rescued the DHCR7-KD-mediated increase in neurogenesis down to the level observed in the control shRNA.
source: The analysis showed that inhibition of GR by RU38486 rescued the DHCR7-KD-mediated increase in neurogenesis down to the level observed in the control shRNA (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Both PD98059 and trametinib efficiently inhibited MEK activation in hNPCs.
source: Indeed, western blots demonstrated that both PD98059 and trametinib efficiently inhibited MEK activation in hNPCs (Figure 8M).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8M.

claim: Both SLOS hNPCs and murine Dhcr7-/- NPCs increased the proportion of βIII+ newborn neurons.
source: As expected, both SLOS hNPCs and murine Dhcr7-/- NPCs increased the proportion of βIII+ newborn neurons, and the MEK inhibition by either PD98058 or trametinib reversed increased neurogenesis with DHCR7 mutations back to the level seen in the wildtype NPCs (Figure 8N, Figure 8—figure supplement 2C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8N and Figure 8—figure supplement 2C, F.

claim: MEK inhibition by either PD98058 or trametinib reversed increased neurogenesis with DHCR7 mutations back to the level seen in the wildtype NPCs.
source: As expected, both SLOS hNPCs and murine Dhcr7-/- NPCs increased the proportion of βIII+ newborn neurons, and the MEK inhibition by either PD98058 or trametinib reversed increased neurogenesis with DHCR7 mutations back to the level seen in the wildtype NPCs (Figure 8N, Figure 8—figure supplement 2C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8N and Figure 8—figure supplement 2C, F.

claim: Coincident TrkB knockdown rescued the increased neurogenesis phenotype observed following shRNA-mediated DHCR7 knockdown.
source: Quantification of EGFP+, βIII-tubulin + cells 3 days later demonstrated that coincident TrkB knockdown rescued the increased neurogenesis phenotype observed following shRNA-mediated DHCR7 knockdown (Figure 8K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8K.

claim: MEK knockdown reversed the premature neurogenesis with DHCR7 shRNA knockdown in human NPCs.
source: Similarly, MEK knockdown also reversed the premature neurogenesis with DHCR7 shRNA knockdown in human NPCs (Figure 8L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8L.

claim: DHCR7 mutations disrupt the normal cortical neurogenesis by hyperactivating RTKs, such as TrkB, through GR activation and thus activating the downstream MEK-ERK1/2 pathway.
source: Thus, DHCR7 mutations disrupt the normal cortical neurogenesis by hyperactivating RTKs, such as TrkB, through GR activation and thus activating the downstream MEK-ERK1/2 pathway.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data showing GR activation, TrkB activation, and rescue by GR or MEK inhibition.

claim: Vitamin E (VE), but not vitamin C (VC), has been shown to effectively inhibit the formation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterols in SLOS patient-derived fibroblasts.
source: In particular, vitamin E (VE), but not vitamin C (VC), has been shown to effectively inhibit the formation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterols in SLOS patient-derived fibroblasts (Korade et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Korade et al., 2014.

claim: Combination of VC with VE, which recycle oxidized VE, enhances the antioxidant activity of VE against lipid peroxidation.
source: Combination with VC, which recycle oxidized VE, enhances the antioxidant activity of VE against lipid peroxidation (Doba et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Doba et al., 1985.

claim: Glutathione (GSH) is an important detoxifying molecule that is abundant (in mM) in cells and can potentially inhibit the formation of DHCEO by reacting with its electrophilic precursor, 7-DHC 5α,6α-epoxide.
source: Furthermore, glutathione (GSH) is an important detoxifying molecule that is abundant (in mM) in cells and can potentially inhibit the formation of DHCEO by reacting with its electrophilic precursor, 7-DHC 5α,6α-epoxide (Porter et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Porter et al., 2020 and Xu et al., 2011.

claim: VE, VE/VC, or GSH, but not VC alone, effectively reversed increased neurogenesis caused by hDHCR7 KD to the level observed in the control.
source: The analysis indicated that VE, VE/VC, or GSH, but not VC alone, effectively reversed increased neurogenesis caused by hDHCR7 KD to the level observed in the control.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data described in the text and shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: Treatments with VE, VE/VC and GSH effectively reduce the increased neurogenesis in both human and murine NPCs with Dhcr7 mutations down to the level observed in WT or Control samples.
source: Treatments with VE, VE/ VC and GSH were again found to effectively reduce the increased neurogenesis in both human and murine NPCs with Dhcr7 mutations down to the level observed in WT or Control samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data described in the text and shown in Figure 8H-I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, B, D, E.

claim: VE, VE/VC, or GSH inhibited the levels of DHCEO in SLOS hiPSCs.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis confirmed that VE, VE/VC, or GSH indeed inhibited the levels of DHCEO in SLOS hiPSCs (Figure 8J).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Free radical chain-breaking antioxidants, such as VE, and nucleophilic antioxidants, such as GSH, can effectively rescue the neurogenesis phenotype observed in SLOS NPCs by inhibiting the free radical oxidation of 7-DHC at different stages.
source: These results suggest that free radical chain-breaking antioxidants, such as VE, and nucleophilic antioxidants, such as GSH, can effectively rescue the neurogenesis phenotype observed in SLOS NPCs by inhibiting the free radical oxidation of 7-DHC at different stages (Figure 8—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing antioxidants rescue the phenotype and reduce DHCEO levels.

claim: β-cyclodextrin treatment reduced cellular cholesterol by more than 50%.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis demonstrated that β-cyclodextrin treatment reduced cellular cholesterol by more than 50% (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A); however, it did not change the proportion of βIII-tubulin+neurons and Ki67 + progenitors either in human NPCs or murine NPCs (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3A.

claim: β-cyclodextrin treatment did not change the proportion of βIII-tubulin+ neurons and Ki67+ progenitors either in human NPCs or murine NPCs.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis demonstrated that β-cyclodextrin treatment reduced cellular cholesterol by more than 50% (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A); however, it did not change the proportion of βIII-tubulin+neurons and Ki67 + progenitors either in human NPCs or murine NPCs (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: Addition of cholesterol did not prevent increased neurogenesis in SLOS NPCs.
source: The results revealed that addition of cholesterol did not prevent increased neurogenesis in SLOS NPCs (Figure 8H–I, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8H-I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, E.

claim: Supplementation of SAG (a Smo agonist) cannot rescue the phenotype with or without cholesterol supplementation in DHCR7-KD hNPCs.
source: Because DHCEO has been shown to inhibit Smo in the Hh signaling pathway (Sever et al., 2016), we also tested whether supplementation of SAG (a Smo agonist) can rescue the phenotype with or without cholesterol supplementation in DHCR7-KD hNPCs (Figure 8G). However, none rescued the neurogenesis phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The lack of cholesterol and inhibition of Hh signaling do not contribute to the neurogenesis phenotype observed in human and murine NPCs with DHCR7 mutations.
source: Thus, the lack of cholesterol and inhibition of Hh signaling do not contribute to the neurogenesis phenotype observed in human and murine NPCs with DHCR7 mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing cholesterol supplementation and SAG treatment do not rescue the phenotype.

claim: The abnormal premature neurogenesis in cortical precursor with Dhcr7 mutations was caused by DHCEO activation of GR and further activation of Trk-mediated neurogenic signaling pathway, but not by the deficiency in cholesterol.
source: Taken together, the abnormal premature neurogenesis in cortical precursor with Dhcr7 mutations was caused by DHCEO activation of GR and further activation of Trk-mediated neurogenic signaling pathway, but not by the deficiency in cholesterol, and inhibition of the formation of DHCEO or GR rescues the neurogenic defects.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the data showing DHCEO activates GR and TrkB, and that antioxidants or GR inhibition rescue the phenotype while cholesterol supplementation does not.

claim: Inhibition of the formation of DHCEO or GR rescues the neurogenic defects.
source: Taken together, the abnormal premature neurogenesis in cortical precursor with Dhcr7 mutations was caused by DHCEO activation of GR and further activation of Trk-mediated neurogenic signaling pathway, but not by the deficiency in cholesterol, and inhibition of the formation of DHCEO or GR rescues the neurogenic defects.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data showing antioxidants (which inhibit DHCEO formation) and GR antagonist rescue the neurogenesis phenotype.

claim: The accumulated 7-DHC-derived oxysterols, particularly DHCEO, disrupt normal embryonic neurogenesis by accelerating progressive depletion of cortical precursors through neurogenesis.
source: Here, we characterized the neurogenic phenotype of SLOS cortical precursors in vitro and in vivo and showed that the accumulated 7-DHC-derived oxysterols, particularly DHCEO, disrupt normal embryonic neurogenesis by accelerating progressive depletion of cortical precursors through neurogenesis, ultimately resulting in greatly reduced cerebral cortex thickness with abnormal cortical layering.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Disruption of normal embryonic neurogenesis by accumulated 7-DHC-derived oxysterols ultimately results in greatly reduced cerebral cortex thickness with abnormal cortical layering.
source: Here, we characterized the neurogenic phenotype of SLOS cortical precursors in vitro and in vivo and showed that the accumulated 7-DHC-derived oxysterols, particularly DHCEO, disrupt normal embryonic neurogenesis by accelerating progressive depletion of cortical precursors through neurogenesis, ultimately resulting in greatly reduced cerebral cortex thickness with abnormal cortical layering.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: DHCR7 mutations promote a significant accumulation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterols in murine and human embryonic cortical NPCs during cortical development.
source: First, LC-MS/MS analyses indicate that DHCR7 mutations promote a significant accumulation of 7-DHC-derived oxysterols in murine and human embryonic cortical NPCs during cortical development.
evidence: This is a summary of the LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2.

claim: DHCR7 is necessary for the normal proliferation of embryonic NPCs and genesis of newborn neurons in culture and within the environment of the embryonic cortex.
source: Second, our studies with KD or KO of DHCR7 indicate that DHCR7 is necessary for the normal proliferation of embryonic NPCs and genesis of newborn neurons in culture and within the environment of the embryonic cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figures 1, 3, 5, and 6.

claim: KD or KO of DHCR7 leads to premature differentiation of cortical precursors to neurons and ultimately a reduction in the thickness of cortical layers through the activation of the neurogenic TrkB-MEK-C/EBP pathway.
source: KD or KO of DHCR7 leads to premature differentiation of cortical precursors to neurons and ultimately a reduction in the thickness of cortical layers. This occurs through the activation of the neurogenic TrkB-MEK-C/EBP pathway.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figures 5 and 6 showing premature neurogenesis and reduced cortical thickness, and Figure 5J-K showing activation of TrkB-MEK-C/EBP pathway.

claim: 7-DHC-derived oxysterols, especially DHCEO, display detrimental effects on normal neural development.
source: Third, we show that 7-DHC-derived oxysterols, especially DHCEO, display detrimental effects on normal neural development, and that DHCEO can activate GR, which is responsible for abnormal cortical precursor differentiation, since DHCR7 KD/KO phenotype can be rescued by concurrent inhibition of glucocorticoid receptor.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 4 showing DHCEO treatment replicates the phenotype.

claim: DHCEO can activate GR, which is responsible for abnormal cortical precursor differentiation.
source: Third, we show that 7-DHC-derived oxysterols, especially DHCEO, display detrimental effects on normal neural development, and that DHCEO can activate GR, which is responsible for abnormal cortical precursor differentiation, since DHCR7 KD/KO phenotype can be rescued by concurrent inhibition of glucocorticoid receptor.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 8 showing DHCEO activates GR and that GR inhibition rescues the phenotype.

claim: DHCR7 KD/KO phenotype can be rescued by concurrent inhibition of glucocorticoid receptor.
source: Third, we show that 7-DHC-derived oxysterols, especially DHCEO, display detrimental effects on normal neural development, and that DHCEO can activate GR, which is responsible for abnormal cortical precursor differentiation, since DHCR7 KD/KO phenotype can be rescued by concurrent inhibition of glucocorticoid receptor.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8D showing GR antagonist rescues the phenotype.

claim: Premature differentiation of cortical precursors with DHCR7 mutations is cholesterol-independent since inhibition of 7-DHC-derived oxysterols via antioxidant treatment can rescue DHCR7 KD/KO phenotype, whereas cholesterol supplementation cannot.
source: Fourth, we show that premature differentiation of cortical precursors with DHCR7 mutations is cholesterol-independent since inhibition of 7-DHC-derived oxysterols via antioxidant treatment can rescue DHCR7 KD/KO phenotype, whereas cholesterol supplementation cannot.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Figure 8 showing antioxidants rescue the phenotype while cholesterol supplementation does not.

claim: DHCEO binds and activates GR, and in doing so, controls the RTK-mediated neurogenic pathway, TrkB-MEK-C/EBP, and thus fate-decision of developing precursors and neurons.
source: Based on these data, we propose a model where DHCEO binds and activates GR, and in doing so, controls the RTK-mediated neurogenic pathway, TrkB-MEK-C/EBP, and thus fate-decision of developing precursors and neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing DHCEO activates GR, which leads to TrkB activation and downstream MEK-C/EBP signaling.

claim: Docking studies provide a structural rationale for DHCEO binding to GR.
source: Although docking studies only approximate enthalpic energies and are an incomplete approximation of affinity, they provide a structural rationale for this activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations and utility of the docking studies performed.

claim: An oxysterol structurally similar to DHCEO, OCDO, can bind and regulate GR and its transcriptional activity.
source: This model is consistent with previous studies showing that an oxysterol structurally similar to DHCEO, OCDO, can bind and regulate GR and its transcriptional activity (Voisin et al., 2017) and ligand-bound GR promoted TrkB phosphorylation, leading to activation of its downstream effectors, MEK and ERK (Jeanneteau et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voisin et al., 2017.

claim: Ligand-bound GR promoted TrkB phosphorylation, leading to activation of its downstream effectors, MEK and ERK.
source: This model is consistent with previous studies showing that an oxysterol structurally similar to DHCEO, OCDO, can bind and regulate GR and its transcriptional activity (Voisin et al., 2017) and ligand-bound GR promoted TrkB phosphorylation, leading to activation of its downstream effectors, MEK and ERK (Jeanneteau et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeanneteau et al., 2008.

claim: The model of DHCEO exerting its effect on neurogenesis through GR does not contradict the previous finding that Wnt/β-catenin inhibition contributes to precocious neurogenesis.
source: Our model of DHCEO exerting its effect on neurogenesis through GR does not contradict the previous finding by Francis et al., which suggests that Wnt/β-catenin inhibition contributes to precocious neurogenesis (Francis et al., 2016), because activation of GR has been shown to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin signaling in several systems (Olkku and Mahonen, 2009; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the compatibility of the current findings with previous work, supported by citations to Francis et al., 2016; Olkku and Mahonen, 2009; and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: Activation of GR has been shown to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin signaling in several systems.
source: Our model of DHCEO exerting its effect on neurogenesis through GR does not contradict the previous finding by Francis et al., which suggests that Wnt/β-catenin inhibition contributes to precocious neurogenesis (Francis et al., 2016), because activation of GR has been shown to inhibit Wnt/β-catenin signaling in several systems (Olkku and Mahonen, 2009; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Olkku and Mahonen, 2009 and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: This work represents the first comprehensive characterization of the neurogenic phenotype in the SLOS mouse model and SLOS patient-derived NPCs.
source: This work represents the first comprehensive characterization of the neurogenic phenotype in the SLOS mouse model and SLOS patient-derived NPCs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The aberrant neural development observed in mice and human NPCs with DHCR7 mutations occurs in a cholesterol-independent and 7-DHC-derived oxysterol-dependent manner.
source: We demonstrate that the aberrant neural development observed in mice and human NPCs with DHCR7 mutations occurs in a cholesterol-independent and 7-DHC-derived oxysterol-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion supported by data showing cholesterol supplementation does not rescue the phenotype while antioxidants do.

claim: Successful rescue of the neurogenic phenotype by inhibiting GR or inhibiting the formation of oxysterols with antioxidants pave the wave for potential therapies for the neurological defects observed in SLOS patients.
source: Successful rescue of the neurogenic phenotype by inhibiting GR or inhibiting the formation of oxysterols with antioxidants pave the wave for potential therapies for the neurological defects observed in SLOS patients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the therapeutic implications of the findings.

claim: GR could be a new therapeutic target against the neurological defects observed in SLOS.
source: These results suggest that GR could be a new therapeutic target against the neurological defects observed in SLOS.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the finding that GR inhibition rescues the neurogenesis phenotype.
